newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa prepares to open the forex taps.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa prepares to open the forex taps.

text.p: For many ordinary South Africans, 35 years of foreign exchange controls will effectively be lifted July 1 when they get a green light to invest overseas for the first time.

A range of offshore unit trusts and foreign currency bank accounts have been lined up to cope with the liberalisation which is expected to meet the needs of all but the very rich, or those emigrating.
Economists expect the new rules will allow inviduals to invest around 150,000 rand ($33,500) offshore.

The exact amount, however, remains a secret -- and with Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals travelling out of the country, some analysts believe Pretoria will keep everyone guessing until the last minute.
For South Africa's financial markets, still edgy after the rand crisis of 1996, these are testing times.

A successful relaxation of controls, coming after evidence of a sharp slowdown in the economy in the first quarter, could pave the way for a cut in the country's punitively high interest rates, boosting stocks and bonds.
But there is a risk: loosening controls could trigger a serious capital flight and hence a fresh run on the rand.

Apprehension about the July 1 move knocked the rand last week and dealers say the market will remain nervous in the near term, with big stop-loss orders waiting to be triggered above 4.50 to the dollar.
Nonetheless, with a consensus emerging that the investment limit will be set at a "safe" level, most economists are sanguine.

Old Mutual Investment Services predicts individuals will be allowed to invest 150,000 rand ($33,500) offshore while the South African Chamber of Business pegs it at between 150,000 ($33,500) and 160,000 ($35,700).
Dave Mohr, chief economist at Old Mutual, estimates there might be 30,000 to 50,000 high net worth individuals wanting to make full use of the allowance.
Others analysts say as many as 100,000 South Africans could rush for the door, suggesting a theoretical outflow of up to 15 billion rand ($3.35 billion).

In practice, most economists see outflows by year-end of less than half that, with few local investors wanting to shift all their funds offshore, especially with domestic markets offering significantly higher returns than investments abroad.
International income funds currently yield around 8 percent compared with around 16 percent in South Africa.

In addition, most of South Africa's ultra-rich have found ways to get around the current exchange control regulations which were introduced in 1961 in the wake of the Sharpeville massacre, when South Africa left the Common Market amid apartheid's strongest hold.

Still, a major outflow by individuals, forcing South African banks to sell rand for dollars, could give fragile confidence a knock -- something the Reserve Bank is only too aware of. Hence the importance of getting bigger reserves in place.

Figures released recently showed South Africa's Reserve Bank held a record 21.8 billion rand ($4.87 billion) of gold and foreign exchange reserves at the end of May, a figure that will be boosted by 1.54 billion rand ($347.4 million) in June following a successful yen bond deal.

In addition, the central bank has access to some 15 billion rand ($3.12 billion) of foreign credit lines, while commercial banks are believed to hold between 5 billion ($1.12 billion) and 10 billion rand ($2.23 billion) in foreign exchange.

The mechanics of the relaxation are also expected to work in the Reserve Bank's favour. The delay in announcing the actual investment limit, coupled with the requirement that all those wishing to invest offshore obtain a tax certificate, suggests bureaucracy will help prevent a rush on day one.
"It's not a once-off event that happens on July 1. ... My guess is you won't be able to assess for three months what the impact will be," said Old Mutual's Mohr.
Increased demand this month for short-term rand option volatilities, derivatives used to hedge risk, suggest many currency players are positioning themselves for potential shock waves.

According to the Reserve Bank's Stals, South Africa has alrady lifted more than half its exchange controls and is committed to lifting remaining restrictions on individuals, corporates and institutions over time.
